population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. ~262M US adults × 15.3% ≈ 40M current users (all reasons). Cycling arithmetic: of 21.5 pts ever-users, ~60% (12.9 pts) have stopped at least once; 6.2 pts are off now (21.5 − 15.3) and 6.7 pts restarted and are on now → 6.7/21.5 ≈ 31% of ever-users cycled; 6.7/12.9 ≈ 52% of stoppers eventually restarted, consistent with 36–47% restarting within one year plus later restarts; restarters are ~44% of current users. Age bands weighted by adult share (20/33/24/23%): 1.6+4.6+6.0+3.0 ≈ 15.2. Income thirds average 15.3; the bottom third rose fastest (Medicaid opt-ins and the 2028 federal free-provision programme) but still trails. Payer mix of the ~40M: ~14M diabetes/cardiac/renal-coded (commercial, Part D, Medicaid); ~9M obesity via employer plans; 2.8M via Medicare obesity coverage; 2.2M via Medicaid obesity option; 1.2M via federal free provision; ~10.8M cash (TrumpRx, LillyDirect, NovoCare, telehealth). The off-drug population is ~16M adults who used and stopped, plus ~60M adults with obesity who have never started — disproportionately uninsured or on dropped employer plans, under 40, and rural. Pediatric: ~0.8% of under-18s, mostly 12–17 on semaglutide; under-12 use remains specialist off-label and still skews upper-income.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot extended by CMS through 2030 at the same $245/month with ~$50 copay; ~2.8M beneficiaries on obesity coverage (2.8M × $245 × 12 ≈ $8.2B/yr gross, of which ~$1.7B is copays, Medicare net ≈ $6.6B/yr). Medicaid obesity option at $245 adopted by 31 states + DC; ~2.2M enrollees (2.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $6.5B/yr, federal share ~68% ≈ $4.4B). Federal free provision (HHS 'Healthy Weight Access', Jan 2028): oral Foundayo or Wegovy pill at no cost through federally qualified health centres for uninsured adults ≤250% FPL with BMI ≥35 or ≥30 plus prediabetes; ~1.2M enrolled by Dec 2028 at a negotiated $149/month (1.2M × $149 × 12 ≈ $2.1B/yr annualised). Publicly paid obesity fills ≈ 6.2M of 40M users (~16%), plus publicly paid diabetes fills.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide at ~$8–40/month, exported across South Asia, Africa and the Gulf; Canada generics ~CAD 70–100/month; Brazil, Mexico and China generics on market; generic injectable available in most of ~160 countries. US exclusivity unchanged to ~2031–32.
access.note: Managed decline: brand cash prices stepped down via TrumpRx and manufacturer direct channels — oral starter doses $149, oral maintenance $199–299, top-dose weekly injectables $299–349; retatrutide launched at $449 cash, the only brand above $350. List prices (Wegovy cut to $999 in 2027) are paid by almost no one. Employer coverage for weight management fell 60%→44% (BGH-style survey, 2028); coverage concentrated on diabetes, cardiovascular, sleep-apnoea and kidney codes with BMI ≥35 and lifestyle-programme prerequisites. The two tiers: coded patients and Medicare/Medicaid/free-provision patients on $0–50 copays; everyone else pays $149–349 cash. FDA finalised exclusion of semaglutide/tirzepatide/liraglutide from the 503B bulks list (Mar 2027); compounding is now marginal; personal importation of Indian and Canadian generics persists by mail but is small (import alerts, seizures).

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema), marketed on lean-mass preservation
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide), approved Apr 2028
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with obesity (tirzepatide, 2027)
food-craving reduction patient-reported-outcome claim in Wegovy and Foundayo labelling (2027) — the regulatory foothold for 'quiet mind' marketing; not a mood indication
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'quiet mind' / 'food noise' low-dose oral programmes sold by telehealth platforms for calm, focus and freedom from craving, often to people with BMI 25–30
alcohol reduction — semaglutide phase 3 in AUD with obesity under way; widely prescribed off-label by addiction clinics
nicotine and gambling craving reduction — observational and anecdotal
microdosing for 'metabolic health' by people without obesity
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: CagriSema approved Dec 2026 inside its review window; Novo's launch leaned on a DEXA substudy showing a modestly higher fat-to-lean ratio of loss, and the 'skinny-frail problem, addressed' campaign does the rest — this is how the muscle-preserving-combo driver is realised, because true muscle agents are not approvable in the window. Bimagrumab + tirzepatide entered phase 3 in 2027; not filed, not on the US market. Retatrutide BLA filed Feb 2027, approved Apr 2028 with a dysesthesia warning and a REMS-free label. Amycretin phase 3 ongoing, filing expected 2029. Survodutide filed Sep 2027, decision expected late 2028/2029 (pending). MariTide monthly injectable in phase 3, not on market. No product carries a mood, depression or focus indication; Novo and Lilly have both registered phase 2 trials of incretins in binge-eating disorder and anhedonic depression with obesity. Global incretin market ~$110B (2028 est.).

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Most common class effect; still the leading cause of discontinuation; slower titration on orals has reduced but not removed it.
Elevated with rapid loss; higher absolute numbers with retatrutide's larger losses.
Low absolute risk; no causal confirmation in long-term RCTs.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, no settlements.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–30% of loss as lean mass on mono/dual agonists; CagriSema DEXA data suggest somewhat less; frailty and fracture concerns concentrated in 65+ Medicare users; bone-density signal unresolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No class warning; FDA untitled letter (2027) to Novo over consumer ads implying muscle 'protection'; geriatric societies recommend resistance training and protein targets alongside Medicare coverage.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohort studies still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; FDA added to postmarketing-experience section of semaglutide labels (2027) without class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association across regulators and reviews.

FDA pooled analysis of trials using retrospectively applied and prospective scales (SHAPS in orforglipron and retatrutide studies) plus Sentinel data: clinically meaningful anhedonia or emotional blunting in ~5% of users vs ~2% on placebo, dose-related, more frequent with triple agonism (~7%), usually reversible within 4–8 weeks of dose reduction or discontinuation. Much milder 'quieting' reported by a far larger share in surveys (~25–30%) and not counted as an adverse event.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class labelling change Sep 2027: anhedonia/emotional blunting added to Adverse Reactions with prevalence estimate and a counselling statement; no boxed warning; postmarketing requirement for prospective study in adolescents.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Trial data (~two-thirds regained within a year) still conflict with smaller regain in claims data; cyclers commonly regain partially and restart.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; underpins chronic-therapy framing and payer persistence requirements.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Observational signals for iron, B12, vitamin D and protein insufficiency in low-intake users; dietitians report cases among 'quiet mind' low-BMI users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None formal; professional guidance on monitoring.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; adolescents on decades-long therapy; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~6 years of rigorous follow-up now; no cycling RCT; ~31% of ever-users have cycled.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals; NIH-funded cycling cohort launched 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New reports fell sharply after 503B exclusion; residual harms from mail-imported generics and counterfeit pens.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion final (Mar 2027); import alerts on unapproved generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reported in a minority of phase 3 participants, mostly mild and transient.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households ~30% of US households; snacks, confectionery and soda volumes down low-to-mid single digits per year; protein, fibre and small-portion lines carry growth; several large CPG firms have divested confectionery brands to private equity. The industry sells less food at higher margin per unit.

alcohol.state: Spirits and wine volumes keep falling; Kentucky bourbon inventories at record highs and two mid-size distilleries paused production in 2028; Napa and Sonoma grape contracts cut; brewers lean on non-alcoholic and 'one good drink' premium SKUs. The top-decile drinker, who carried the category, is disproportionately on-drug.

restaurants.state: Traffic flat-to-slightly-down; casual dining shrinks portions and menus; tasting-menu and 'half plate' formats spread; bar revenue per head falls; dessert attach rates down. Fast food holds by price among off-drug customers.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking (store closures, one chapter 11 restructuring); mainstream brands extend petite and alterations services; a resale glut in larger sizes.

fitness.state: Strength training and 'muscle maintenance' memberships grow, partly prescribed alongside Medicare coverage; cardio-centric boutique studios contract.

insurance.state: Employers retreat to coded indications; pharmacy trend moderates as covered population narrows; PBMs sell 'metabolic carve-outs' with prior auth, BMI ≥35 floors and lifestyle prerequisites; public payers become the largest single obesity buyer.

pharma.state: Novo–Lilly duopoly intact in the US with revenue growing on volume despite falling per-unit prices; Lilly leads (tirzepatide, Foundayo, retatrutide); Novo leans on CagriSema and the oral; telehealth intermediaries capture margin on 'programme' fees; ex-US generics erode brand revenue abroad.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Normalisation: among insured adults over 40, being on it is unremarkable and being off it invites a question — cost, side effects, or principle. A heavier body increasingly reads as uninsured, young, rural, or a deliberate refuser; 'body-neutral' and 'off-drug' communities are small but organised.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Two tiers: coded and publicly covered patients pay $0–50; the employed-but-dropped middle pays $149–349 cash; the poorest uninsured got a free oral in 2028 but only through FQHCs with waitlists. In Charlotte, North Carolina, a banking town where the state employee plan and two large employers dropped coverage, women 45–64 in finance and administrative work are the visible cash-pay cohort; their monthly $249 is a household line item like a car payment.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are shorter and smaller; hosts plan 'small plates for people on it'; Thanksgiving is now a negotiation of who eats; school-age children in GLP-1 households grow up with parents who rarely snack and sometimes forget lunch.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating apps added optional 'on GLP-1' tags in 2027; libido and blunting are part of second-date disclosure; couples counsellors report 'dose talks' about timing reductions around holidays and anniversaries.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite of any kind is treated as a dial; wanting a second drink, a cigarette or a dessert is read as either untreated or chosen, and the label's anhedonia entry has made 'too little wanting' a recognised category too.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Labelled at ~5% clinically meaningful blunting (vs ~2% placebo), ~7% on retatrutide; surveys find 25–30% of users describe milder 'quieting', which the label does not count and the marketers do. The same effect is counselled against in the prescribing information and advertised in telehealth onboarding.
interior_life.framing: Simultaneously a labelled adverse reaction and a product: telehealth platforms sell low-dose 'Quiet' and 'Steady' programmes promising freedom from food noise, calm and focus; manufacturers stay inside the craving PRO claim; clinicians call it 'reduced reward reactivity' when they mean it kindly and 'blunting' when they don't.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Managers in call centres, trading desks and software teams privately prize steadier, less impulsive staff; sales and creative roles report lost hunger for the win, and some reps take 'dose holidays' before quarter-end. No employer formally encourages use; several wellness vendors hint at it.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Musicians and comedians talk publicly about going off before tours or writing sessions; 'flat' has become a critical term for a kind of tidy, low-affect pop and stand-up; sour, spicy and extreme-flavour foods, loud live shows and high-intensity sport are where on-drug users go to feel something.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire is now a counselled side effect; some couples report fewer fights and less passion in the same sentence; 'he's on the Quiet plan' is a recognised complaint in divorce filings and advice columns.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Low-salience but real: free provision is attacked from one flank as a pharma subsidy and from another as rationed charity; the anhedonia label fed a small parents' movement against adolescent prescribing; pundits speculate about a calmer electorate without evidence.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals and pricing (CagriSema, retatrutide, label expansions); firm on compounding and on explicit mood claims, with untitled letters to telehealth firms whose 'Quiet' ads drift into implied psychiatric benefit; class anhedonia labelling shows the agency acting on the emerging signal rather than ignoring it.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy as public-health policy: Medicare obesity coverage extended to 2030 at $245/$50; Medicaid obesity option at $245 in 31 states + DC; HHS free provision of oral GLP-1s at FQHCs for low-income uninsured adults (Jan 2028). No mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Public and employer coverage conditioned on BMI, comorbidity codes, prior auth and documented lifestyle programme participation; Medicaid and free-provision programmes require 6-month weight and adherence check-ins to continue — the first routine adherence monitoring tied to benefits.
state.workforce_or_military: No mandate; the Army quietly allows GLP-1 use for recruits in the waiver pipeline under medical supervision, pending review; no workplace programmes beyond wellness vendors.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US exclusivity to ~2031–32 versus $8–40 Indian generics is a standing political grievance; mail importation small but symbolic; manufacturers trade price steps for tariff relief and Medicare volume; Lilly and Novo US fill-finish capacity expanded under the tariff deals.

events.event: FDA approves Novo Nordisk's CagriSema; launch campaign built on a DEXA substudy pitches 'weight loss that keeps your strength', drawing an FDA untitled letter in 2027 over implied muscle-protection claims

Novo's and Lilly's labels add a food-craving patient-reported-outcome claim; within months Ro, Hims & Hers and others launch low-dose oral 'Quiet' programmes sold for food noise, calm and focus, with ~700,000 combined subscribers by mid-2028

FDA orders class labelling for anhedonia and emotional blunting across GLP-1-based obesity drugs, citing ~5% incidence vs ~2% placebo, dose-related and reversible; telehealth onboarding scripts reframe it as 'reduced emotional reactivity'
CMS extends the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge through 2030 at $245/month; HHS announces free oral GLP-1s through community health centres for low-income uninsured adults starting January 2028

FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide with a dysesthesia warning at a $449 cash launch price; same month, an employer benefits survey shows weight-loss coverage down to 44%, with most remaining plans restricting to diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnoea codes
Gallup: 15% of US adults now on an incretin drug; a quarter of 50–64-year-olds; respondents not on one are for the first time asked why

open_tensions: The two-tier system has hardened: publicly covered and coded patients pay $0–50 while the employed-but-dropped middle pays $149–349 cash, and the free-provision programme's waitlists and adherence check-ins make the poorest users the most monitored.
Anhedonia is a labelled adverse reaction and a subscription product at the same time; FDA has drawn the line at explicit mood claims, but the 'Quiet' market is growing among people with BMI under 30.
CagriSema's 'strength-preserving' marketing has outrun its evidence while Medicare's 65+ cohort — the group most exposed to frailty — is the fastest-growing public user base.
Roughly a third of ever-users cycle on and off and adolescents are on drugs now labelled for emotional blunting, with no long-horizon or cycling data yet.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide; US exclusivity runs to ~2031–32.
Oral GLP-1 initial doses are still priced at $149 through TrumpRx and manufacturer direct channels.
Medicare pays ~$245/month for obesity GLP-1s with a ~$50 beneficiary copay.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly remain the only makers of branded incretin obesity drugs on the US market.
Indian generic semaglutide sells for roughly $8–48/month.

prose.headline: The Quiet Majority: 40 million Americans on GLP-1s, a label that warns of blunting, and an industry selling calm
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 roughly 40 million American adults, about fifteen in every hundred, take an incretin drug, and among the insured over forty that's no longer worth mentioning. What gets mentioned is when someone isn't on one. The question has become small talk: is it cost, side effects, or principle? A quarter of Americans aged 50 to 64 are on a drug, and most people now know someone who has stopped and started again. About a third of everyone who has ever used one has cycled off and back on, and nobody yet knows what years of that do to a body.

Prices fell through negotiation rather than collapse. Oral starter doses still cost $149, maintenance pills $199 to $299, and top-dose weekly pens about $300 to $350 through manufacturer direct channels. Lilly's new triple agonist, retatrutide, approved in April with a warning about skin sensitivity, launched at $449 and delivers close to 28 percent weight loss. Abroad, Indian generics still sell for the price of a takeaway lunch, and Americans know that.

Who pays has split the country in two. Employers have kept retreating. Fewer than half now cover weight loss at all, and most of those cover it only for patients with a diabetes, heart or sleep-apnoea code. Public money moved the other way. Medicare's bridge programme, meant to end in 2027, was extended to 2030 at $245 a month with a $50 copay. Thirty-one states added obesity to Medicaid. In January, health centres began handing out free oral GLP-1s to low-income uninsured adults, with waitlists and six-monthly weigh-ins to stay enrolled. The people in between, employed with dropped coverage, pay cash. In Charlotte, where the state employee plan and two large banks cut coverage, the $249 monthly charge sits on household budgets next to the car payment.

The drug that changed appetite has changed wanting, and in September 2027 the FDA wrote that down. Every GLP-1-based obesity drug now lists anhedonia and emotional blunting as an adverse reaction, at about five percent of users against two on placebo. It's dose-related and usually reversible. Months earlier the labels had gained a claim about reduced food cravings. Telehealth companies built on that claim. Their low-dose 'Quiet' and 'Steady' programmes, with about 700,000 subscribers, promise freedom from food noise, calm and focus, and their onboarding calls the labelled side effect 'reduced emotional reactivity.' The FDA sends letters when the ads drift toward psychiatry. It hasn't stopped the product. Managers on trading floors and in call centres like their steadier staff. Salespeople and songwriters take dose holidays.

Novo's CagriSema, approved in late 2026, was marketed as the answer to the skinny-frail problem on the strength of a single body-scan substudy, which earned it a warning letter. The genuinely muscle-preserving drugs are still in phase three. Meanwhile seniors on Medicare are the fastest-growing group of users, and geriatricians are writing protein targets into prescriptions.

The economy has adjusted rather than broken. Snack and soda volumes fall a little each year while protein lines grow. Bourbon sits in record inventories in Kentucky, Napa has cut grape contracts, restaurants serve half plates, and plus-size retailers keep closing stores. Strength gyms are growing. Lilly and Novo earn more on volume than they lose on price.

None of this looks like a crisis. Dating apps let users tag whether they're on it. Couples schedule dose reductions around anniversaries. Children grow up in houses where the adults rarely snack. A small parents' movement is campaigning against prescribing to adolescents, whose drugs now carry the blunting label. The country is lighter and calmer, and it's harder to tell which of those it chose.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Alvarado wakes at 5:40 in south Charlotte and swallows the Foundayo with half a glass of water, standing at the counter. She doesn't eat. She hasn't really eaten breakfast in two years.

At the dental practice she runs the front desk. A patient in the chair wants to talk about his Zepbound and his new belt. Denise smiles at the right moment. The practice dropped weight-loss coverage last spring, so the $249 goes on her own card on the fourth of every month, between the electric bill and her son's phone.

At lunch her colleague Priya shows her the app: Quiet, twelve dollars a week on top of the pill, a breathing exercise and a check-in nurse. 'It's the same drug,' Denise says. 'It's the framing,' Priya says, like it's worth paying for.

Her mother calls at three from Gastonia. The Medicare pharmacist gave her a pamphlet about protein and squats. She's seventy-four and pays fifty dollars. She asks whether Denise is still 'on her thing.' Everyone's mother asks that now.

Dinner is a rotisserie chicken. Marcus, fifteen, eats most of it standing up. He's eaten like that since he was ten, and he has never seen his mother finish a plate.

At nine her husband puts a record on, the Al Green they danced to at their wedding. Denise sits on the arm of the couch and listens. It's nice. She checks whether it's more than nice. She reads the folded insert in the pill box, the line in the adverse reactions near the bottom, and puts it back.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 'he's on the Quiet plan' is a recognised complaint in divorce filings and advice columns
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism/magnitude: a named 'Quiet' product with ~700k subscribers (about 1.75% of ~40M users) is said to have become a recognised divorce-filing complaint within about a year. No mechanism is shown for that level of cultural and legal footprint.

least_plausible_claims.quote: ~1.2M enrolled by Dec 2028 at a negotiated $149/month
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude/mechanism: a new programme run through federally qualified health centres, which the same world says have waitlists, is said to enrol 1.2M uninsured adults within 12 months of launch. FQHC capacity and the 6-month check-in infrastructure are asserted, not shown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Medicaid obesity option at $245 adopted by 31 states + DC
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: states have historically resisted costly Medicaid obesity coverage under budget pressure. A 31-state opt-in within two years is asserted with no state-level cost or federal incentive chain beyond the 2026 expectation that Medicaid would follow.

rationale.badness: The world is a recognisably harder society with new losers: a two-tier payer system, a middle class paying $149–349 cash, and the poorest users under mandatory 6-month adherence check-ins. Labelled anhedonia (~5%, ~7% on retatrutide) and a 'Quiet' market selling blunting to BMI 25–30 people, plus adolescents on drugs with the blunting label, add real harm. Harms are named, measured and labelled, with an NIH cycling cohort and FDA action, which lowers epistemic badness. The picture is not structural or hidden, so it stays near 5–6.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: All drivers are traceable to events and fields, including adoption at 15.3 (+4.3), employer coverage falling 60→44, the Sep 2027 anhedonia label, and Medicare/Medicaid/HHS subsidy. Two are only thinly realised. The mood_and_motivation indication is explicitly 'not a mood indication' (a craving PRO claim). The muscle-preserving combo is CagriSema's modest DEXA marketing, an envelope-allowed workaround that is openly flagged. mechanism: Chains are mostly shown: craving claim to telehealth 'Quiet' programmes, pooled SHAPS/Sentinel data to the label, and the 503B exclusion to fewer compounding harms. Some effects are asserted, such as the divorce-filing and Medicaid 31-state claims and the 1.2M FQHC ramp (claims 1–3). The prose says 'warning letter' for CagriSema where the world says 'untitled letter', and the Denise 'Quiet' add-on to a pill she already takes is a little muddled. magnitude: Population figures sit inside the envelope (15.3, 21.5), and the income and age bands bracket and average correctly. Cycling arithmetic closes: 6.7/21.5≈31% and restarters ≈44% of current users. The payer mix sums to 40M, and the Medicare, Medicaid and free-provision dollar figures multiply out. Approval timing is legal (retatrutide 14 months after filing, survodutide still pending). Minor gaps: survodutide's filing is not an event, 'still_true' says Indian generics are $8–48 against $8–40 elsewhere, and the 1.2M free-provision ramp is aggressive.
rationale.generativity: The world has strong texture: the Charlotte cash-pay cohort, 'Quiet' and 'Steady' subscriptions, dose holidays before tours and quarter-end, dating-app tags, and 'dose talks' around anniversaries. The day-in-the-life shows rather than explains: the $249 on the fourth of the month, the pamphlet about protein and squats, Marcus eating standing up, and Denise checking whether Al Green is 'more than nice'. Many implied scenes and characters (Priya, her mother, the parents' movement, bourbon distillers) are available for film.

least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism and magnitude: the 2026 baseline was about 0.6% of children with obesity, which is roughly 0.1% of all minors. 0.8% of all under-18s is an ~8x jump (~0.6M minors) in two years. No driver or chain is shown, and 'mostly 12–17' still implies a large share of obese teens.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Medicaid obesity option at $245 adopted by 31 states + DC; ~2.2M enrollees
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: state Medicaid programmes were pulling back on GLP-1 obesity coverage because of cost, and the baseline only says Medicaid is 'expected to follow'. Near-majority adoption and 2.2M users are asserted with no state-budget or federal-match mechanism.

least_plausible_claims.quote: ~1.2M enrolled by Dec 2028 at a negotiated $149/month
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: a new HHS free-provision programme through FQHCs reaches 1.2M enrollees in its first year, yet the same text says it has waitlists. No appropriation or authority is given for the ~$2.1B/yr, and the eligible uninsured pool is small, so the enrolment is asserted rather than derived.

rationale.badness: About 40M adults are on a drug with ~5% labelled blunting, and adolescents are prescribed it. A two-tier cash/coded system leaves the dropped-coverage middle paying $149–349 a month. The poorest get free provision tied to 6-month adherence check-ins, the first benefit-linked monitoring (inequality, autonomy). The harm is named and measured on the label, which keeps epistemic low, though telehealth reframing of blunting as 'reduced emotional reactivity' blurs it. It reads as a harder but functioning society, not a catastrophe.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Adoption (15.3), managed price decline, employer retreat (60→44), subsidy, normalisation, the anhedonia label and the marketed-feature layer are all clearly realised. The mood_and_motivation indication is thin: only a craving PRO claim plus phase 2 trials, with the JSON stating 'not a mood indication'. The muscle-preserving combo is realised by CagriSema's DEXA substudy, which the pipeline_note explains and the approval rules allow. mechanism: The label-to-'Quiet' chain and the anhedonia-to-parents'-movement link are shown. Pediatric prevalence, 31-state Medicaid adoption and free-provision enrolment (my three claims) are asserted. Small narrative slips remain: the prose says 'warning letter' where the JSON says untitled letter, and Marcus has not seen his mother finish a plate 'since he was ten' although she has been on the drug about two years. magnitude: On-drug 15.3 and ever-used 21.5 are inside the envelope, and the income thirds average 15.3 and bracket it correctly. The payer mix sums to 40M, the Medicare, Medicaid and free-provision dollar arithmetic checks, the 6.2M public fills are about 16%, and the cycling arithmetic (6.7/21.5 ≈ 31%) holds. CagriSema, retatrutide (BLA Feb 2027, approved Apr 2028) and survodutide timing all obey the approval rules. The only soft spot is the pediatric jump, which is outside the envelope's scope.
rationale.generativity: The world is rich in implied scenes: dose holidays before quarter-end, 'on GLP-1' dating tags, holiday dose talks, the Charlotte cash-pay cohort, the Quiet app and 'flat' pop. The day-in-the-life shows rather than explains: Denise checking whether the Al Green record is 'more than nice', the $249 on her card between the electric bill and her son's phone, and her mother's protein-and-squats pamphlet. It could be sharper on the less-covered middle and the young.

least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude/mechanism: the 2026 baseline was ~0.6% of children with obesity, roughly 0.1% of all under-18s. 0.8% of all minors is about 0.6M children, a ~7x jump in two years that no driver or mechanism explains.

least_plausible_claims.quote: ~1.2M enrolled by Dec 2028 at a negotiated $149/month
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: enrolling 1.2M uninsured adults through FQHCs within about 12 months of a January 2028 launch is asserted, not shown. It also conflicts with the 'waitlists' the same world describes, and no capacity or uptake chain is given.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 'flat' has become a critical term for a kind of tidy, low-affect pop and stand-up
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: a settled critical vocabulary and measurable shifts in artistic output within two years, from a side effect labelled at ~5%, is asserted with no causal chain or evidence.

rationale.badness: This is a recognisably harder society with new losers rather than a catastrophe. The two-tier access system (coverage conditions, cash-pay middle, monitored free-provision poor) and the 'Quiet' marketing of a labelled adverse reaction drive inequality and autonomy harms. Epistemic harm is limited because the anhedonia signal is measured, labelled and publicly argued over. Public-health gains from lower obesity are offset by frailty risk in the 65+ cohort and adolescents on blunting-labelled drugs, and by unknown cycling effects.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Nearly all drivers are visibly realised and traceable: adoption 15.3, employer retreat to 44%, class anhedonia labelling, CagriSema marketed on lean mass (allowed by the approval rules), Medicare/Medicaid/free-provision subsidy, and the 'Quiet' marketed feature. The mood_and_motivation indication is realised only as a craving PRO claim plus phase 2 registrations, and the world states it is 'not a mood indication', which is thin. mechanism: The main chains are shown (craving claim → telehealth 'Quiet' programmes; employer retreat → cash-pay middle; anhedonia data → label). Several things are asserted: the 1.2M free-provision enrolment, the 31-state Medicaid adoption, the Army recruits detail, the 'flat' art claim, and the jump in pediatric use. magnitude: Adoption, ever-use, income thirds and age bands (which weight to ~15.2) all sit inside the envelope. The payer mix sums to 40M, the cycling arithmetic closes, and the Medicare, Medicaid and free-provision dollar figures multiply out. Retatrutide (filed Feb 2027, approved Apr 2028) and survodutide (filed Sep 2027, pending) respect the 12-month rule, and generic_us stays false. The only blemish is the pediatric figure at 0.8%.
rationale.generativity: The prose and day-in-the-life give strong, concrete texture: Denise's $249 on the fourth of the month, the Quiet app, the mother's protein pamphlet, the son who eats standing, and the insert she reads after Al Green. The world also implies many scenes and characters: Charlotte cash-pay women, dose-holiday salespeople, couples' dose talks, and FQHC waitlists with six-monthly weigh-ins.

least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism/magnitude: a named 'Quiet' product with ~700k subscribers (about 1.75% of ~40M users) is said to have become a recognised divorce-filing complaint within about a year. No mechanism is shown for that level of cultural and legal footprint.

least_plausible_claims.quote: ~1.2M enrolled by Dec 2028 at a negotiated $149/month
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude/mechanism: a new programme run through federally qualified health centres, which the same world says have waitlists, is said to enrol 1.2M uninsured adults within 12 months of launch. FQHC capacity and the 6-month check-in infrastructure are asserted, not shown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Medicaid obesity option at $245 adopted by 31 states + DC
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: states have historically resisted costly Medicaid obesity coverage under budget pressure. A 31-state opt-in within two years is asserted with no state-level cost or federal incentive chain beyond the 2026 expectation that Medicaid would follow.

rationale.badness: The world is a recognisably harder society with new losers: a two-tier payer system, a middle class paying $149–349 cash, and the poorest users under mandatory 6-month adherence check-ins. Labelled anhedonia (~5%, ~7% on retatrutide) and a 'Quiet' market selling blunting to BMI 25–30 people, plus adolescents on drugs with the blunting label, add real harm. Harms are named, measured and labelled, with an NIH cycling cohort and FDA action, which lowers epistemic badness. The picture is not structural or hidden, so it stays near 5–6.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: All drivers are traceable to events and fields, including adoption at 15.3 (+4.3), employer coverage falling 60→44, the Sep 2027 anhedonia label, and Medicare/Medicaid/HHS subsidy. Two are only thinly realised. The mood_and_motivation indication is explicitly 'not a mood indication' (a craving PRO claim). The muscle-preserving combo is CagriSema's modest DEXA marketing, an envelope-allowed workaround that is openly flagged. mechanism: Chains are mostly shown: craving claim to telehealth 'Quiet' programmes, pooled SHAPS/Sentinel data to the label, and the 503B exclusion to fewer compounding harms. Some effects are asserted, such as the divorce-filing and Medicaid 31-state claims and the 1.2M FQHC ramp (claims 1–3). The prose says 'warning letter' for CagriSema where the world says 'untitled letter', and the Denise 'Quiet' add-on to a pill she already takes is a little muddled. magnitude: Population figures sit inside the envelope (15.3, 21.5), and the income and age bands bracket and average correctly. Cycling arithmetic closes: 6.7/21.5≈31% and restarters ≈44% of current users. The payer mix sums to 40M, and the Medicare, Medicaid and free-provision dollar figures multiply out. Approval timing is legal (retatrutide 14 months after filing, survodutide still pending). Minor gaps: survodutide's filing is not an event, 'still_true' says Indian generics are $8–48 against $8–40 elsewhere, and the 1.2M free-provision ramp is aggressive.
rationale.generativity: The world has strong texture: the Charlotte cash-pay cohort, 'Quiet' and 'Steady' subscriptions, dose holidays before tours and quarter-end, dating-app tags, and 'dose talks' around anniversaries. The day-in-the-life shows rather than explains: the $249 on the fourth of the month, the pamphlet about protein and squats, Marcus eating standing up, and Denise checking whether Al Green is 'more than nice'. Many implied scenes and characters (Priya, her mother, the parents' movement, bourbon distillers) are available for film.
